name: Mongol Empire

fields.foundation: The Mongol Empire was founded in the early 13th century on the steppes of Mongolia by Genghis Khan, born Temüjin around 1162. The steppe was then divided among rival Mongol and Turkic tribes, among them the Tatars, Keraits, Merkits and Naimans. He unified them through alliances, military skill and ruthless suppression of opponents, and was proclaimed Genghis Khan at a kurultai (assembly) in 1206. Tradition credits him with a body of law known as the Yassa, though its exact form is uncertain. Two things made the empire's rise possible: the steppe way of life, which produced highly mobile and disciplined mounted archers, and the divisions among its settled neighbours, the Western Xia, the Jurchen Jin dynasty in northern China and the newly expanded but poorly integrated Khwarazmian Empire in Central Asia. Control of pastures and trade routes added to its economic and military capacity. Genghis Khan broke up old tribal loyalties, reorganised his followers into new decimal units and promoted commanders for loyalty and ability. This gave him centralised authority over a flexible tribal hierarchy and made possible rapid and sustained conquest across Asia and into Europe.
fields.socioeconomy: Mongol society rested on a pastoral nomadic economy, organised around extended families, herds and seasonal migration. Horses, camels, sheep, goats and cattle provided food, transport and military advantage, while trade supplied grain, silk, ceramics and metals that the steppe could not produce. The Borjigin royal clan and a warrior aristocracy stood at the top of society. Common herders did most of the economy's work, and captives, including many skilled artisans, were transferred from conquered lands. Conquered cities kept their administrative, craft and commercial functions and so linked sedentary economies to the Mongol network. The new capital at Karakorum, founded under Ögedei in the 1230s, drew merchants and craftsmen from across Eurasia. The Mongols imposed taxation and tribute in grain, textiles and precious metals, supported by censuses across the empire. They encouraged long-distance trade through partnerships with merchant associations (ortogh) and protected it under the Pax Mongolica. Travel along the routes connecting China, the Middle East and Europe became relatively safe, and the economies of Eurasia were linked more closely than ever before.
fields.military: The Mongol military was highly organised, disciplined and mobile. Its core was mounted archers drawn from the steppe tribes, augmented by units from conquered peoples. Armies were divided into decimal units (arban, zuun, mingghan, tumen) for command and control, which kept them flexible at any size. Tactics included feigned retreats, coordinated multi-pronged assaults and the extensive use of siege engines operated by Chinese and Persian engineers. Genghis Khan's campaign against the Khwarazmian Empire (1219–1221) showed mastery of logistics, reconnaissance and psychological warfare. The generals Subutai and Jebe defeated the Rus and Kipchaks at the Kalka River in 1223, and Subutai later led the western campaign that devastated the Rus principalities and defeated Polish and Hungarian armies at Legnica and Mohi in 1241. Hülegü's campaign in the Middle East destroyed Baghdad in 1258. The army relied on promotion by merit, strict discipline and rapid communication through the yam relay system. Cavalry used speed, manoeuvrability and coordinated archery to overcome numerically superior opponents. Military power was the main instrument of expansion, of political consolidation and of the enforcement of tribute across Eurasia.
fields.governance: Government of the Mongol Empire was centred on the Great Khan, elected by a kurultai of the royal family, but relied on extensive delegation to princes, subordinate khans and regional administrators. The Yassa, traditionally attributed to Genghis Khan, provided a framework for military discipline and social order, and the adoption of the Uyghur script gave the Mongols their first written administration. Conquered peoples supplied bureaucrats such as the Khitan minister Yelü Chucai, engineers and tax collectors, while resident overseers known as darughachi supervised local rulers and revenue. Diplomatic correspondence and the yam relay network made government over great distances possible. The Mongols generally tolerated diverse faiths, granting tax exemptions to clergy in return for prayers for the khan. After the succession war between Kublai and Ariq Böke (1260–1264), the Golden Horde, Ilkhanate, Chagatai Khanate and Yuan dynasty operated as largely independent states, though they continued to acknowledge a shared Chinggisid heritage. Central legitimacy, delegated administration and pragmatic tolerance allowed the empire to hold together, for a time, across lands and peoples more diverse than any state before it had ruled.
fields.impact: The Mongol Empire changed Eurasian history by making possible trade and cultural and technical exchange across the continent on a new scale. By securing the overland routes under the Pax Mongolica, it allowed goods, ideas and people to travel between China, the Middle East and Europe, from merchants such as Marco Polo to envoys such as the Franciscan William of Rubruck, and encouraged exchanges in astronomy, medicine, cartography and gunpowder technology. The same networks may also have helped carry the Black Death westwards in the 1340s. The Mongols influenced successor states by combining steppe traditions with sedentary administration, above all in Yuan China and the Ilkhanate of Persia, where Rashid al-Din compiled a pioneering world history. Population movements, including the transfer of skilled artisans and administrators, accelerated cultural integration. Mongol campaigns redrew political boundaries: they destroyed the Khwarazmian Empire, the Jin and Song dynasties and the Abbasid Caliphate, and subjected the Rus principalities to more than two centuries of tributary rule. Mongol patronage of commerce and communication prepared the wider networks of exchange of the Late Middle Ages.
fields.decline: The unified Mongol Empire began to fragment in the mid-13th century, through overextension, succession disputes and the difficulty of governing very large territories. After the death of the Great Khan Möngke in 1259, the succession war between Kublai and Ariq Böke and conflicts between the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate broke the empire into independent khanates pursuing separate policies. Kublai's death in 1294 removed the last Great Khan widely recognised across the empire. Further succession struggles, rebellions in China and Persia, and economic strains, including inflation of Yuan paper currency, famines and the ravages of plague, reduced the khanates' capacity to sustain armies and tribute networks. The Ilkhanate disintegrated after Abu Sa'id's death in 1335, and the Yuan dynasty was driven from China in 1368 by the Ming, founded by Zhu Yuanzhang, a leader who had risen in the Red Turban Rebellion. The Golden Horde fractured into rival khanates and lost its hold over Muscovy, an end marked symbolically by the Great Stand on the Ugra River in 1480. Mongol khans persisted in the steppe, but the empire had long ceased to function as a single polity. Its collapse showed the limits of steppe-based rule over diverse and sedentary populations.
fields.summary: The Mongol Empire was the steppe power that, from Genghis Khan's unification of the tribes in 1206, joined China, the Middle East and Europe in a single network of trade and exchange under the Pax Mongolica. Its break-up into rival khanates showed the limits of steppe-based rule over large settled populations.
fields.teaser: The Mongol Empire remains history's largest contiguous land empire. Its Pax Mongolica allowed trade and exchange across Eurasia on a new scale, connecting civilisations from China to Europe.
fields.t0: Genghis Khan united the steppe tribes in 1206 and built the largest contiguous land empire in history.
fields.t1: Under the Pax Mongolica, protected trade routes linked China, the Middle East and Europe as never before.
fields.t2: Succession wars split it into rival khanates after 1260; the Yuan fell to the Ming in 1368.
fields.dyk: The Mongols generally tolerated diverse faiths, even granting clergy tax exemptions in return for prayers for the khan.
